title: DEALING WITH CONTENTION
subtitle: Many users want the same thing at the same moment. Exactly one should win, every time.
footer: Theory: DDIA ch 7 Transactions · DDIA ch 8 Trouble with distributed systems

items: Limited resources: seats, stock, a username, a driver, the highest bid.
Any "check, then act" sequence that two requests can run at the same time.
Check-then-act from two users: both see AVAILABLE, both book. A race condition (DDIA Ch 7 write skew).
Make the check and the write one atomic statement. The database guarantees only one succeeds.
Other tools: pessimistic lock (high contention), optimistic version check (low contention), distributed lock with TTL (holds across services), or a per-item queue (extreme contention).

head: Tool
Use when
rows: Single row, single DB: the default
Multi-step logic on few rows, high contention
Temporary holds across services (seat hold, driver lock)

items: Can the check and the write be one statement? Use a conditional UPDATE (… WHERE status = AVAILABLE). This is the default.
Multi-step logic on a few rows with high contention? SELECT … FOR UPDATE, locking rows in a fixed order.
Low contention? Optimistic concurrency with a version column; retry on conflict.
A temporary hold that spans services? A lock with a TTL (Redis SET NX EX), plus a fencing token if correctness depends on it.
Extremely hot single item? Serialize requests through a queue partitioned by item.

blocks.text: "The check and the write must be atomic, so the hold is a single conditional UPDATE. One row updated means you got the seat; zero means someone else did."

items: Holding database locks while waiting on a human (payment, form).
Trusting a distributed lock without fencing when a paused process could wake up later.

blocks.text: Used in: Rate limiter, Online auction, Ticketmaster
